## Introduction

tidycreel gives fisheries biologists a tidy, pipe-friendly way to design and
analyse creel surveys. You work with the terms used in the field (dates,
strata, counts, interviews) without handling the internals of the survey
package.

This tutorial analyses one complete season, start to finish. A clerk worked a
lake for 120 days, from May 1 to August 28. On 36 of those days the clerk made
an instantaneous count of anglers and interviewed angling parties, both those
that had finished fishing and some still fishing. The
questions are the usual ones: how much fishing happened over the season, how
many fish were caught, and how many were kept.

Each answer is built from the one before:

```
calendar -> design
counts             -> effort        (angler-hours)
interviews         -> catch rate    (fish per angler-hour)
effort x rate      -> total catch   (fish)
```

## The season

```{r data}
library(tidycreel)

data(example_season_calendar)
data(example_season_counts)
data(example_season_interviews)

head(example_season_calendar)
table(example_season_calendar$day_type, example_season_calendar$sampled)
```

The calendar lists every day of the season, not only the sampled ones, and
splits them into weekdays and weekends. The clerk sampled 28 of the 86
weekdays and 8 of the 34 weekend days. That list of every day is what lets
tidycreel expand from the days that were sampled to the whole season.

## Survey design

```{r design}
design <- creel_design(example_season_calendar, date = date, strata = day_type)
design
```

`creel_design()` uses tidy selectors, so you name columns without quotes. The
design records the 120-day calendar and its two strata.

## Counts

```{r counts}
head(example_season_counts)

design <- add_counts(design, example_season_counts,
  count_col = total_anglers,
  period_length_col = daylight_hours
)
```

Each row is one instantaneous count: the number of anglers fishing at the
moment the clerk looked. A count is a number of anglers, not an amount of
effort. To turn it into effort, tidycreel needs to know how much time the count
stands for. Here the single count on each day represents the whole 14-hour
fishing day, so `daylight_hours` is the period length. Effort for a day is the
count times that length, in angler-hours.

Leaving out `period_length_col` still gives an estimate, but its unit is
unknown, and `estimate_effort()` warns that no period length was supplied.
tidycreel derives units from what you give it and never assumes one.

## Effort

There are two different questions you can ask of these counts.

```{r effort}
estimate_effort(design)
estimate_effort(design, target = "period_total")
```

The first estimate, the default, is the effort **on the 36 days that were
sampled**: 3,066 angler-hours. The second is the effort **over the whole
120-day season**, about 9,994 angler-hours. That season total is the number
usually reported. Each stratum's mean daily effort is multiplied by the number
of days in that stratum, then the strata are added. For a season total, ask for
`target = "period_total"`.

The standard error comes from the day-to-day variation among the sampled days
within each stratum. With one count per day there is no separate within-day
term: the error in each day's single count is already part of the variation
between days, so `se_within` is 0 by construction, not because activity was
steady through the day. It becomes non-zero when a day has several counts
(`vignette("effort-pipeline")`).

Estimates can be broken down by any column in the design with `by`:

```{r effort-by}
estimate_effort(design, by = day_type, target = "period_total")
```

The 86 weekdays account for most of the season's effort, about 7,900
angler-hours to the weekends' 2,100. Per day, the two are closer: about 92
angler-hours on an average weekday and 61 on an average weekend day.

## Interviews

```{r interviews}
head(example_season_interviews)

design <- add_interviews(design, example_season_interviews,
  catch = catch_total,
  harvest = catch_kept,
  effort = hours_fished,
  trip_status = trip_status,
  n_anglers = n_anglers
)
```

Each row is one party. `add_interviews()` checks the interviews as it attaches
them, and here it raises one warning: 153 of the 231 parties caught nothing.
That is not an error in these data. Most anglers on most fisheries go home
without a fish, and those zeros belong in the catch rate. The warning is there
because, on a real data sheet, a column of zeros can also mean a catch that was
never recorded. If your zeros are real, as these are, there is nothing to fix.

`n_anglers` matters. `hours_fished` is how long the party fished, so it is in
party-hours. A party of three fishing two hours put in six angler-hours, and
`n_anglers` lets tidycreel make that conversion. The catch rate is then in fish
per angler-hour, the same footing as the counts. Without it the rate would be
per party-hour, which cannot be multiplied by effort in angler-hours.

## Catch rates

```{r rates}
estimate_catch_rate(design)
estimate_harvest_rate(design)
```

The catch rate is about 0.22 fish per angler-hour, and the harvest rate about
0.06. Both are ratio-of-means estimates, total catch divided by total effort
across the interviews. By default they use only the 172 complete trips.
A party interviewed while still fishing is more likely to be met the longer it
stays, so incomplete trips over-represent long trips (length-of-stay bias) and
give a biased catch rate unless the rate is steady through a trip. `vignette("incomplete-trips")` covers when and how
incomplete trips can be used.

## Total catch and harvest

```{r totals}
estimate_total_catch(design, target = "period_total")
estimate_total_harvest(design, target = "period_total")
```

A total is effort times rate, with the uncertainty of both carried into its
standard error. The unit follows: angler-hours times fish per angler-hour is
fish. About 2,230 fish were caught over the season, and about 650 were kept.
These totals take `target` too, and need `target = "period_total"` for the
season, just as effort does.

Totals break down the same way as effort:

```{r totals-by}
estimate_total_catch(design, by = day_type, target = "period_total")
```

Released fish come from species-level catch records, attached with
`add_catch()`, rather than from the interview totals; see
`?estimate_total_release`.

## Using results as data

An estimate prints with its method, variance method and unit. It is not itself
a data frame, so dplyr verbs do not work on it directly. Convert it first.
`as_tibble()` returns one row per estimate, with the metadata copied into
columns so it stays attached to every row:

```{r as-tibble}
catch_by_day <- estimate_total_catch(design, by = day_type, target = "period_total")
catch_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(catch_by_day)
catch_tbl

catch_tbl[catch_tbl$day_type == "weekend", c("day_type", "estimate", "se", "unit")]
```

`as.data.frame()` does the same for base R. Use `metadata = FALSE` for the
estimates table alone.

## Plotting

Estimates have an `autoplot()` method that draws each estimate with its
confidence interval:

```{r plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Point estimates of total catch on weekdays and weekends, with 95 percent confidence intervals."}
ggplot2::autoplot(catch_by_day)
```

`vignette("visualisation")` covers the other plots.

## Variance methods

Standard errors use Taylor linearization by default. Bootstrap and jackknife
replicates are also available, for effort and for every estimate built on it:

```{r variance}
set.seed(123)
estimate_effort(design, target = "period_total", variance = "bootstrap")
estimate_effort(design, target = "period_total", variance = "jackknife")
```

- **Taylor linearization** (default) is fast and appropriate for most
  estimates.
- **Bootstrap** resamples sampled days. Use it to check the linearization or
  for statistics that are not smooth.
- **Jackknife** is deterministic, so it gives the same answer on every run.

`vignette("replicate-designs")` compares them.

## Next steps

This tutorial used the most common design: instantaneous counts and access
interviews, with weekday and weekend strata. From here:

- `vignette("survey-scheduling")` builds the sampling calendar before the
  season, including high-use periods such as openers.
- `vignette("interview-estimation")` and `vignette("incomplete-trips")` cover
  catch-rate estimators in depth.
- `vignette("section-estimation")` handles lakes split into sections.
- The **Survey Types** articles cover bus-route, ice, camera, aerial and
  mark-recapture designs.
- `vignette("glossary")` defines the terms used throughout.
